output.myth: When Aun cut the string, the sky went off up the wind and left the boats below to the Gale. A woman called Hatun was out with her two children when Tavo came down laughing and filled the hull. She did not pray. She bailed with her gourd, the one she used for broth, until her wrists were bark and the children lay quiet in the bottom of the boat. Tavo laughed and blew harder. Hesk, who keeps count at the pole, counted every scoop. At dawn the boat was still afloat, though Hatun was not. Ennu the Kite-Wright sewed her into sailcloth and hung her gourd up beside her, so something would keep bailing the dark. Look for it low in the south, over the water, where the sky is half seen. Each drop that flies off the lip is one she would not let go down. Keep your scoop by the door. Tavo does not forgive, but he does get bored.
output.verse:
The gourd hangs low south,
still she bails the black cold dark,
bail till morning comes.
